case.dispatchHook: Tracking glitch at the Cape. Stars, moons and comets filed in the wrong groups.
briefing: Agent, the tracking room at Cape Canaveral lost its object catalog overnight.
The Sun is filed as a planet, two moons are listed as comets, and a launch is waiting on the fix.
Sort the objects back into their groups, then check what the sky is really doing.
The launch window will not move, so work carefully.

lab.intro: The catalog lost its groups. Read each object card and send it to the group it belongs in.

bins.name: Star
bins.hint: A star is a huge ball of hot gases that gives off its own light.

bins.name: Planet
bins.hint: A planet is a large, round object that travels around the Sun.

bins.name: Moon
bins.hint: A moon travels around a planet.

bins.name: Small body
bins.hint: Asteroids and comets are small objects that travel around the Sun.

cards.name: The Sun
card: Gives off its own light and heat
Sits at the center of the solar system
cards.why: The Sun makes its own light from hot gases, so it is a star.

cards.name: Sirius
card: Looks like a tiny point because it is so far away
cards.why: Sirius makes its own light and only looks small because it is very far away, so it is a star.

cards.name: Earth
card: Travels around the Sun once a year
Has liquid water on its surface
cards.why: Earth is a large, round object that travels around the Sun, so it is a planet.

cards.name: Jupiter
card: Giant ball of gas with bands of clouds
Travels around the Sun beyond the asteroid belt
cards.why: Jupiter is a giant object that travels around the Sun, so it is a planet.

cards.name: Titan
cards.why: Titan travels around the planet Saturn, so it is a moon.

cards.name: Phobos
cards.why: Phobos travels around the planet Mars, so it is a moon.

cards.name: Vesta
card: Rocky chunk in the belt between Mars and Jupiter
cards.why: Vesta is a rocky chunk in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, so it is an asteroid, a small body.

cards.name: Halley's Comet
card: Made of ice, dust and rock
Grows a glowing tail near the Sun
cards.why: Halley's Comet is an icy object that grows a tail near the Sun, so it is a comet, a small body.

case.debriefClosed: Case closed. The catalog is sorted, and the launch is back on the board.
case.debriefOpen: Case stays open for now. The sky comes back as a cold case soon, and it will still be there.

items.stem: A science museum on the Space Coast shows a model of a galaxy. A small arrow on the model marks where our Sun is. Which list best describes what a galaxy is made of?
options: one star and the planets that travel around it
only planets and their moons
clouds of water vapor and rain
gas, dust, and many stars
why: Decoy: one star with its planets is a solar system, which is only a tiny part of a galaxy.
Decoy: a galaxy is mostly stars, gas, and dust, not just planets and moons.
Decoy: water vapor and rain belong to Earth's weather, not to a galaxy.
Correct: a galaxy is a huge group of gas, dust, and many stars, and our Sun is one of those stars.
items.alt: A spiral galaxy seen at an angle, with a small arrow marking our Sun's place.
items.tisCheck: Conceptual galaxy only; the galaxy's name is not assessed; objects orbiting stars are not assessed; no star counts or distances.
items.misconceptions: A galaxy confused with the solar system; a galaxy thought to be only planets.

items.stem: From Earth, the Sun looks much larger and brighter than any other star. Which statement best explains why?
options: The Sun is the closest star to Earth.
The Sun is the largest star in the galaxy.
The Sun is the only star that gives off light.
The other stars give off light only at night.
why: Correct: the Sun looks large and bright because it is much closer to Earth than any other star.
Decoy: many stars are larger than the Sun, but they are so far away that they look tiny.
Decoy: every star gives off its own light.
Decoy: stars shine all the time, but in the day the Sun's light hides them.
items.alt: Two stars drawn the same size, one near Earth and bright, one far away and faint, with a small Earth.
items.tisCheck: Star appearance in relation to distance only; no numeric distances; the Sun's effects on Earth are not assessed.
items.misconceptions: The Sun believed to be the biggest star; other stars thought not to make light or to shine only at night.

items.stem: Star A and Star B give off the same amount of light. Seen from Earth, Star B looks much dimmer than Star A. Which is the best explanation?
options: Star B is a planet, not a star.
Star B is much farther from Earth than Star A.
Star B has stopped giving off light.
Star B is made of rock instead of gas.
why: Decoy: both are stars that give off light, and planets do not make their own light.
Correct: a star that is farther away looks dimmer, even when it gives off the same amount of light.
Decoy: a star that gave off no light could not be seen at all.
Decoy: stars are made of hot gases, not rock.
items.alt: Two stars drawn the same size: Star A near Earth and bright, Star B far away and faint, with a small Earth.
items.tisCheck: Star brightness in relation to distance; stars made of gases with no chemical makeup; no numbers.
items.misconceptions: Dim stars thought to be dying, small, or planets.

items.stem: A poster at a Space Coast museum shows three things in space: Earth, our solar system, and our galaxy. Which list goes from smallest to largest?
options: galaxy, solar system, Earth
solar system, Earth, galaxy
Earth, solar system, galaxy
Earth, galaxy, solar system
why: Decoy: this list goes from largest to smallest.
Decoy: Earth is one planet inside the solar system, so the solar system cannot be smaller than Earth.
Correct: Earth is part of the solar system, and the solar system is a tiny part of the galaxy.
Decoy: the galaxy holds many stars, and our whole solar system is only one small part of it.
items.alt: A spiral galaxy seen at an angle, with a small arrow marking where our Sun is.
items.tisCheck: Conceptual galaxy only (a galaxy holds many stars, our Sun among them); no numbers; the galaxy name is not assessed.
items.misconceptions: The solar system and the galaxy treated as the same size or swapped.

items.stem: A student points to a star in the night sky and asks what it is made of. Which answer is correct?
options: ice and rock
hot gases
liquid water
solid metal
why: Decoy: ice and rock make up comets and asteroids, not stars.
Correct: a star is a huge ball of hot gases that gives off its own light.
Decoy: liquid water could not last on something as hot as a star.
Decoy: a star is not a solid object.
items.alt: Two stars drawn the same size, one near and bright, one far away and faint.
items.tisCheck: Stars are made of gases; no chemical makeup is named.
items.misconceptions: Stars pictured as rocky or icy objects like planets or comets.

items.stem: At noon, the sky over Tampa is bright and no stars can be seen. At night, many stars appear. Which statement best explains why stars cannot be seen during the day?
options: Stars stop giving off light during the day.
Stars move to the other side of the galaxy during the day.
Clouds always cover the stars during the day.
Stars still shine, but the Sun's light makes the sky too bright to see them.
why: Decoy: stars give off light all the time, day and night.
Decoy: stars do not travel across the galaxy each day, so they are still there at noon.
Decoy: many days have clear skies, and the stars are still hidden.
Correct: the Sun is the closest star, and its bright light hides the dimmer stars that are much farther away.
keyWords: cannot be seen during the day
items.alt: Earth with a lit half facing the Sun at the left and a dark half facing away, with an arrow showing Earth spinning.
items.tisCheck: Stars give off visible light; brightness in relation to distance; no numbers; the Sun's effects on Earth are not assessed.
items.misconceptions: Stars thought to shine only at night or to go away during the day.

items.stem: Leo builds a model of the inner planets for a Space Coast museum. He needs to place Earth in the model. Counting out from the Sun, which planet is Earth?
options: the first planet
the second planet
the third planet
the fourth planet
why: Decoy: the first planet from the Sun is Mercury.
Decoy: the second planet from the Sun is Venus.
Correct: Earth is the third planet from the Sun, after Mercury and Venus.
Decoy: the fourth planet from the Sun is Mars.
items.alt: The Sun at the left with four inner planets in a row, none of them labeled.
items.tisCheck: Earth's position in the solar system; no distances, no interactions between objects.
items.misconceptions: Earth assumed to be the first planet or the one in the middle.

items.stem: The table describes two planets in our solar system. Which statement is most likely true?
options: Planet A is an outer planet, and Planet B is an inner planet.
Both planets are inner planets.
Planet B is a star because it is so large.
Planet A is an inner planet, and Planet B is an outer planet.
why: Decoy: this is backward, since the outer planets are the large gas planets with rings.
Decoy: inner planets are rocky and have no rings, so Planet B cannot be one.
Decoy: a planet does not become a star by being large, because stars give off their own light.
Correct: small and rocky fits the inner planets, and large, gassy, and ringed fits the outer planets.
items.alt: A table: Planet A is rocky, smaller than Earth, with no rings; Planet B is made of gas, much larger than Earth, with rings.
items.tisCheck: Inner vs outer planet characteristics (SC.5.E.5.2); no numbers, no interactions between objects.
items.misconceptions: Inner and outer planets reversed; large objects assumed to be stars.

items.stem: A tracking room at Cape Canaveral logs four objects in our solar system. Which object is a moon?
options: Object 1
Object 2
Object 3
Object 4
why: Correct: a moon travels around a planet, and Object 1 travels around Mars.
Decoy: Object 2 travels around the Sun and is made mostly of gas, so it is a planet.
Decoy: Object 3 sits at the center and gives off its own light, so it is the Sun, a star.
Decoy: Object 4 grows a tail near the Sun, so it is a comet.

visual.title: Tracked Objects
rows: Small and rocky, no light of its own
Hot gases, gives off its own light
Ice and dust, grows a tail near the Sun

items.alt: A table of four objects: one travels around Mars, one is a huge gas object that travels around the Sun, one stays at the center and gives off light, and one grows a tail near the Sun.
items.tisCheck: Telling the Sun, a planet, a moon and a comet apart by their characteristics; no gravity or other interactions assessed.
items.misconceptions: Any object near a planet or the Sun called a planet; comets and moons confused.

items.stem: Scientists track two small objects. Object 1 is made of rock and metal and travels in a belt between Mars and Jupiter. Object 2 is made of ice, dust, and rock and forms a glowing tail near the Sun. Which statement names both objects correctly?
options: Object 1 is a comet, and Object 2 is an asteroid.
Object 1 is an asteroid, and Object 2 is a comet.
Both objects are moons because they are small.
Both objects are planets because they travel around the Sun.
why: Decoy: this swaps them, since comets are icy with tails and asteroids are rock and metal.
Correct: asteroids are rock and metal in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, and comets are icy and form tails near the Sun.
Decoy: a moon travels around a planet, and being small does not make an object a moon.
Decoy: many objects travel around the Sun, but these small ones are not planets.
items.alt: The Sun at the left with a band of small rocky objects in a belt farther out.
items.tisCheck: Asteroid vs comet characteristics; no interactions between objects, no numbers.
items.misconceptions: Asteroids and comets swapped; small objects called moons; anything that travels around the Sun called a planet.

items.stem: A student lists ways the Sun is different from the planets. Which statement is correct?
options: The Sun gives off its own light, and the planets do not.
The Sun travels around Earth once a day.
The Sun is a planet made of rock.
The Sun is smaller than Jupiter.
why: Correct: the Sun is a star that makes its own light, and the planets only reflect sunlight.
Decoy: the Sun only seems to move across the sky each day because Earth spins.
Decoy: the Sun is a star made of hot gases, not a rocky planet.
Decoy: the Sun is much larger than Jupiter, the largest planet.
items.alt: The Sun at the left with Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars in a row.
items.tisCheck: Sun vs planet characteristics; the Sun's effects on Earth are not assessed; no numbers.
items.misconceptions: The Sun moving around Earth; the Sun treated as a planet; Jupiter thought to be bigger than the Sun.

items.stem: A space probe launched from Florida will fly past one of the outer planets. Which planet could it be?
options: Mars
Venus
Neptune
Mercury
why: Decoy: Mars is the last of the inner planets, just before the asteroid belt.
Decoy: Venus is an inner planet close to the Sun.
Correct: Neptune is an outer planet, far beyond the asteroid belt.
Decoy: Mercury is the inner planet closest to the Sun.
items.alt: The Sun at the left, the four small inner planets near it, and the four large outer planets farther out.
items.tisCheck: Inner vs outer planets by position (SC.5.E.5.2); no distances or numbers.
items.misconceptions: Mars thought to be far out; the order of the planets unclear.

items.stem: In Miami, the Sun rises in the morning and sets in the evening. Which motion causes day and night on Earth?
options: the Sun traveling around Earth
Earth spinning on its axis
Earth traveling around the Sun
the Moon blocking the Sun each night
why: Decoy: the Sun only seems to move because Earth spins.
Correct: as Earth spins, Miami turns toward the Sun for day and away from it for night.
Decoy: one trip around the Sun takes a year, not a day.
Decoy: the Moon does not block the Sun every night.
items.alt: Earth with a lit half facing the Sun at the left and a dark half facing away, with an arrow showing Earth spinning.
items.tisCheck: Day and night from rotation; apparent motion only; no seasons, no tilt.
items.misconceptions: The Sun traveling around Earth; rotation and revolution mixed up.

items.stem: Kim records where the Sun is in the sky at three times on one day. Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky?
options: The Sun travels around Earth once each day.
Earth travels around the Sun once each day.
Earth spins, so the Sun appears to move from east to west.
Wind pushes the Sun across the sky.
why: Decoy: the Sun does not travel around Earth; it only appears to move.
Decoy: Earth takes a whole year, not a day, to travel around the Sun.
Correct: as Earth spins, the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
Decoy: wind is moving air on Earth, and it cannot move the Sun.
items.alt: A table: at 9 a.m. the Sun is low in the east, at noon it is high in the sky, and at 3 p.m. it is lower in the west.
items.tisCheck: Apparent movement of the Sun from Earth's rotation; no seasons, no directness of sunlight.
items.misconceptions: Apparent motion taken as real motion of the Sun; a day confused with a year.

items.stem: Jay draws the Moon's shape every few nights. The lit part grows until the Moon looks like a whole circle. Then it shrinks until he cannot see the Moon at all. About how long does it take before the pattern starts again?
options: about one day
about one week
about one year
about one month
why: Decoy: one day is how long Earth takes to spin once.
Decoy: in one week the Moon goes through only part of its changes.
Decoy: one year is how long Earth takes to travel around the Sun.
Correct: the Moon's shape goes through its whole pattern in about one month.
items.alt: Eight small Moon shapes in a row, growing from dark to a whole lit circle and shrinking back.
items.tisCheck: The Moon's observable shape over about a month; no causes of the changes and no names for the shapes.
items.misconceptions: The Moon's pattern confused with a day, a week or a year.

items.stem: In winter, Ava sees a star pattern called Orion in the evening sky over Gainesville. In summer, she looks at the same time of night and cannot find it. Which statement best explains this?
options: Earth travels around the Sun, so the night sky shows different stars in different seasons.
The stars in Orion stop shining in the summer.
Earth spins faster in the summer, so Orion goes by too quickly.
Clouds always hide Orion in the summer.
why: Correct: as Earth moves around the Sun, the night side of Earth faces different stars, so star patterns change with the seasons.
Decoy: the stars in Orion shine all year long.
Decoy: Earth spins at the same speed all year.
Decoy: Florida has many clear summer nights, and Orion still is not seen.
items.alt: A table: in winter at 9 p.m., Orion is high in the sky; in summer at 9 p.m., Orion is not seen.
items.tisCheck: Star patterns change with the seasons; the formal word for a named star group is not used; no causes of seasons, no tilt.
items.misconceptions: Stars turning off; Earth spinning at different speeds; weather blamed for a pattern that is not there.

items.stem: Earth and the Moon are always moving. Which of these takes about one year?
options: Earth spinning once on its axis
the Moon traveling once around Earth
the Sun rising and setting once
Earth traveling once around the Sun
why: Decoy: one spin of Earth takes about one day.
Decoy: the Moon travels around Earth in about one month.
Decoy: the Sun rises and sets once each day because Earth spins.
Correct: Earth takes about one year to travel once around the Sun.
items.alt: The Sun, Earth on its path around the Sun, and the Moon on its smaller path around Earth, with arrows.
items.tisCheck: Earth's rotation and revolution and the Moon's revolution; no causes of seasons or of the Moon's shapes.
items.misconceptions: Rotation and revolution confused; the Moon's month mixed up with a year.

items.stem: At 8 p.m., a camper at a Florida state park sees a bright star low in the eastern sky. At midnight, the same star is high in the sky. Which statement best explains why the star seemed to move?
options: The star traveled across the galaxy in four hours.
Earth traveled halfway around the Sun in four hours.
Earth spun during those four hours, so the star appeared to move.
The Moon pulled the star higher in the sky.
why: Decoy: a star does not move far enough in one night to cross our sky, so the motion comes from Earth.
Decoy: a trip around the Sun takes a year, so Earth moves only a tiny part of the way in four hours.
Correct: stars appear to rise in the east and cross the sky because Earth spins, just like the Sun does.
Decoy: the Moon does not move the stars.
items.alt: A table: at 8 p.m. the star is low in the east, at 10 p.m. it is partway up the sky, and at midnight it is high in the sky.
items.tisCheck: Apparent movement of stars from Earth's rotation; no numeric distances; the formal word for a named star group is not used.
items.misconceptions: Stars moving on their own; rotation and revolution confused.

codex.title: Sirius
codex.line: Sirius gives off more light than our Sun, but it looks like a tiny point because it is so far away.

codex.title: Phobos
codex.line: Phobos is a small, lumpy moon that travels around Mars.

codex.title: Halley's Comet
codex.line: Halley's Comet comes near the Sun about once every 76 years, and its ice makes a glowing tail.
